title: Before and after
job: Time clauses: while, until, since, already, not yet
verifiedBy: Claude Opus 5 — LLM review, authorised by repo owner

allowedPatterns: Seitdem ich hier wohne + , + V-2 + ich
Ich bin noch nicht fertig + , + aber + <clause>

rules.text: GERMAN SPLITS THE PHRASE FROM THE CLAUSE, and you already own half of every pair. English while, until, before and since each introduce either a noun or a whole clause; German uses a different word for each. während plus a noun is L3-M8's genitive preposition, während plus a subject and a verb is the conjunction written here. seit plus a noun is L3-M7's; seitdem plus a clause is this module's. bis plus a time is L2-M6's goodbye; bis plus a clause is until. The half you own is not the half this module teaches.

ALL SIX CONJUNCTIONS ARE VERB-FINAL. bevor, während, seitdem, bis, sobald and solange send the verb of their own clause to the end, exactly as weil and dass do (L1-M9). Put that clause first and the whole clause counts as position one, so the main clause inverts behind the comma: Bevor ich ins Büro gehe, trinke ich einen Kaffee — comma, verb, subject. That is L3-M3's fronting law, now with six more words that trigger it.

bevor TAKES THE SAME TENSE IN BOTH HALVES. English shifts the tense across the join — before I leave I will have had a coffee — and German refuses to: both verbs stay in the present, or both go into the Perfekt together. There is no sequence of tenses to keep, and an anglophone who builds one has written a sentence no German would.

seitdem PAIRS WITH THE PRESENT for anything still going on. English needs a perfect — since I have lived here — and German uses the plain present: Seitdem ich hier wohne, fahre ich weniger Auto. This is L3-M7's seit rule doing its second job, on a clause instead of a noun, and it is the only tense seitdem takes while the state continues.

THE ASPECT ADVERBS ARE ONE SYSTEM, and it is the half of this module that is not a clause at all. schon is already, noch is still, noch nicht is not yet, nicht mehr is no longer. English carries three of those four with a perfect tense and a negation; German carries all four with a small adverb and a plain present. nicht mehr sits exactly where nicht sits, at the end of the middle field.

erst IS THE ONE WITH NO ENGLISH WORD AT ALL. erst um acht is not until eight; schon um acht is as early as eight. Same clock time, two opposite judgements about it, and English needs a negation to say one of them. erst is L4-M1's row and keeps its note there; schon is L2-M2's, inside the noch row. This module writes both and opens neither.

bis IS WRITTEN HERE AND OPENS NO ROW. L2-M6 owns bis, in the goodbye Bis Freitag, so a learner tapping bis during practice is shown that note rather than this one. Both seats are the same until — the older note is incomplete, not wrong — and this sentence's own deconstruction still puts the conjunction on the page in front of the learner.

sentences.display: Bevor ich ins Büro gehe, trinke ich einen Kaffee
sentences.cue: Before I go to the office, I have a coffee
sentences.literal: Before I into-the office go, drink I a coffee

words.note: Verb-final, and both halves keep the SAME tense: Bevor ich gehe, trinke ich. Never *bevor ich werde gehen.

sentences.trap: English shifts the tense across before — before I leave I will have a coffee. German leaves both verbs in the present and the order alone carries the sequence.
sentences.sound: buh-FOR ikh ins bue-ROH GAY-uh, TRIN-kuh ikh EYE-nun KA-fay.

variations.display: Ich trinke einen Kaffee, bevor ich ins Büro gehe
variations.cue: I have a coffee before I go to the office
variations.changed: The bevor clause moved to the back, so nothing is fronted and the main clause keeps its plain V-2 order: Ich trinke.

mistake.display: Bevor ich werde ins Büro gehen, trinke ich einen Kaffee
mistake.why: German has no sequence of tenses after bevor. The present does the work in both halves; a future here is English grammar wearing German words.

sentences.usage: Describing the fixed order of two everyday things.
sentences.mnemonic: bevor puts the verb last and the tense unchanged.

sentences.display: Während ich koche, kann ich nicht gleichzeitig telefonieren
sentences.cue: While I am cooking I cannot be on the phone at the same time
sentences.literal: While I cook, can I not at-the-same-time telephone

words.note: The adverb that spells out what während already implies. It sits in the middle field, never first: kann ich nicht gleichzeitig …

sentences.trap: während plus a noun is the genitive preposition of L3-M8 (während der Woche). Here it takes a subject and a verb, and the verb goes to the end.
sentences.sound: VAY-rent ikh KOKH-uh, kan ikh nikht GLYKH-tsy-tikh tay-lay-fo-NEE-run.

variations.display: Ich kann nicht gleichzeitig kochen und telefonieren
variations.cue: I cannot cook and be on the phone at the same time
variations.changed: No clause at all: two infinitives under one modal, and gleichzeitig alone carries the simultaneity.

mistake.display: Während ich koche, kann ich nicht telefonieren gleichzeitig
mistake.why: gleichzeitig is a middle-field adverb, not a tail. It belongs before the infinitive that closes the bracket, never after it.

sentences.usage: Turning down a call, or explaining why two things do not fit into one moment.
sentences.mnemonic: während holds two clocks in one clause.

sentences.display: Wir müssen eine Stunde warten, bis der Zug kommt
sentences.cue: We have to wait an hour until the train comes
sentences.literal: We must an hour wait, until the train comes

words.note: Feminine: die Stunde, eine Stunde. A length of time takes no preposition in German — eine Stunde warten, not *für eine Stunde.

sentences.trap: bis here is the conjunction until, not the goodbye Bis Freitag that L2-M6 taught. Same word, and tapping it in practice will show you that older note.
sentences.sound: veer MUE-sun EYE-nuh SHTOON-duh VAR-tun, bis dair tsook KOMT.

variations.display: Wir warten hier, bis der Zug kommt
variations.cue: We are waiting here until the train comes
variations.changed: The length drops out and the modal with it; bis and its verb-final clause are untouched.

mistake.display: Wir müssen eine Stunde warten, bis kommt der Zug
mistake.why: bis is a subordinating conjunction, so its own verb goes to the very end: bis der Zug kommt. Only a main clause puts the verb second.

sentences.usage: On a platform, telling somebody how long the wait is.
sentences.mnemonic: bis holds the door open until the verb arrives last.

sentences.display: Seitdem ich hier wohne, fahre ich weniger Auto
sentences.cue: Since I have been living here I drive less
sentences.literal: Since I here live, drive I less car

words.note: Takes a clause and the PRESENT while the state lasts: Seitdem ich hier wohne. With a noun the word is seit (L3-M7).
The comparative of wenig, and it never changes its ending: weniger Auto, weniger Zeit, weniger Leute.

sentences.trap: English needs a perfect after since — since I have lived here. German uses the plain present, because the living is still going on.
sentences.sound: ZYT-daym ikh here VOH-nuh, FAA-ruh ikh VAY-nig-er OW-toh.

variations.display: Seitdem ich hier wohne, gehe ich mehr zu Fuß
variations.cue: Since I have been living here I walk more
variations.changed: mehr for weniger — the other end of the same comparison, and the seitdem clause is untouched.

mistake.display: Seitdem ich hier gewohnt habe, fahre ich weniger Auto
mistake.why: A Perfekt after seitdem says the living has stopped. While it is still true, German keeps the present — the tense is what marks it as ongoing.

sentences.usage: Explaining a change that started at a point and is still true.
sentences.mnemonic: seitdem starts the clock and the present keeps it running.

sentences.display: Ich bin noch nicht fertig, aber es dauert nicht lange
sentences.cue: I am not ready yet, but it will not take long
sentences.literal: I am still not ready, but it lasts not long

words.note: Two words German keeps in this order, and together they are one idea. Its opposite is schon: schon fertig against noch nicht fertig.
Impersonal: es dauert lange, es dauert eine Stunde. German uses the present for something still to come — no will needed.

sentences.trap: English says not yet with a perfect — I have not finished yet. German says it with the present and two small adverbs, and nothing about the tense changes.
sentences.sound: ikh bin nokh nikht FAIR-tikh, AA-ber es DOW-ert nikht LANG-uh.

variations.display: Ich bin schon fertig, es dauert nicht mehr lange
variations.cue: I am ready already; it will not take much longer
variations.changed: schon replaces noch nicht and nicht mehr replaces nicht — the same sentence moved to the far end of the aspect system.

mistake.display: Ich bin nicht noch fertig, aber es dauert nicht lange
mistake.why: The order is fixed: noch nicht is not yet, nicht noch is nothing at all. German writes the still before the not.

sentences.usage: Asking somebody to give you another minute.
sentences.mnemonic: noch nicht: the still comes first, the not comes second.

sentences.display: Ich arbeite nicht mehr in Berlin, sondern zu Hause
sentences.cue: I no longer work in Berlin, but at home
sentences.literal: I work not more in Berlin, but-rather at home

words.note: One idea in two words, and it sits where nicht sits. Its opposite is noch: Ich arbeite noch hier against Ich arbeite nicht mehr hier.
The but that corrects a no. After nicht, German needs sondern, not aber: nicht in Berlin, sondern zu Hause.

sentences.trap: English has one but and German has two. aber adds a contrast to something true; sondern replaces something you just denied, and only a negative can license it.
sentences.sound: ikh AR-by-tuh nikht mair in ber-LEEN, ZON-dern tsoo HOW-zuh.

variations.display: Ich arbeite noch in Berlin, aber nicht mehr jeden Tag
variations.cue: I still work in Berlin, but no longer every day
variations.changed: noch for nicht mehr in the first half, so the second half takes aber — nothing was denied for sondern to correct.

mistake.display: Ich arbeite nicht mehr in Berlin, aber zu Hause
mistake.why: The first half denied Berlin, so the second half is a replacement, not a contrast. A replacement after a negative takes sondern.

sentences.usage: Correcting somebody's picture of where you are these days.
sentences.mnemonic: aber adds, sondern replaces — and only a no can call for sondern.

sentences.display: Sobald ich zu Hause bin, rufe ich Sie an
sentences.cue: As soon as I am home I will call you
sentences.literal: As-soon-as I at home am, call I you on

words.note: Verb-final like bevor, and like bevor it stays in the present for something still to come: Sobald ich zu Hause bin.

sentences.trap: English cannot use a future after as soon as either, but it can in the main clause: I will call. German simply leaves both halves in the present.
sentences.sound: zoh-BALT ikh tsoo HOW-zuh bin, ROO-fuh ikh zee AN.

variations.display: Ich rufe Sie an, sobald ich zu Hause bin
variations.cue: I will call you as soon as I am home
variations.changed: The clause moved to the back; the separable prefix an still closes the main clause, and nothing else moves.

mistake.display: Sobald ich werde zu Hause sein, rufe ich Sie an
mistake.why: sobald behaves like bevor: the present carries the future. A werde here is the English will translated word for word.

sentences.usage: Promising to get back to somebody the moment you can.
sentences.mnemonic: sobald is bevor pointing the other way, with the same tense.

sentences.display: Solange es regnet, bleiben wir hier
sentences.cue: As long as it is raining we are staying here
sentences.literal: As-long-as it rains, stay we here

words.cue: as long as, for as long as
words.note: The conjunction is written solid; so lange as two words is the adverb so long. Verb-final, and it marks a condition that lasts.

sentences.trap: solange is one word and so lange is two, and the space changes the part of speech. The conjunction never takes a space.
sentences.sound: zoh-LANG-uh es RAYG-net, BLY-bun veer here.

variations.display: Wir bleiben hier, solange es regnet
variations.cue: We are staying here as long as it is raining
variations.changed: The clause moved behind, so the main clause opens with its subject and needs no inversion.

mistake.display: Solange es regnet, wir bleiben hier
mistake.why: A fronted clause fills position one, so the main verb must come next: bleiben wir, not wir bleiben. This is the comma-verb-subject law.

sentences.mnemonic: solange: one word, one stretch of time.

sentences.display: Inzwischen ist es schon halb neun
sentences.cue: By now it is already half past eight
sentences.literal: Meanwhile is it already half nine

words.cue: by now, meanwhile, in the meantime
words.note: Marks the time that has passed since something else. In first position it inverts the verb, like every fronted adverb.

sentences.trap: halb neun is half past EIGHT — German counts towards the coming hour, not back from the past one. That is L2-M6's clock, still true here.
sentences.sound: in-TSVISH-un ist es shone halp NOYN.

variations.display: Inzwischen ist es erst halb neun
variations.cue: It is only half past eight so far
variations.changed: erst for schon: the same clock time judged as early rather than late. erst is L4-M1's row and keeps its note there.

mistake.display: Inzwischen es ist schon halb neun
mistake.why: inzwischen is in first position, so the verb takes second and the subject follows it: Inzwischen ist es. V-2 does not care that the first word is an adverb.

sentences.usage: Noticing out loud that time has got away from you.
sentences.mnemonic: inzwischen is the gap between then and now, in one word.

sentences.display: Am Ende des Tages bin ich immer müde
sentences.cue: At the end of the day I am always tired
sentences.literal: At-the end of-the day am I always tired

words.note: Neuter: das Ende. am Ende is the fixed phrase for in the end, and it takes the dative without thinking about it.

sentences.trap: des Tages is L3-M8's genitive, not a new case. The whole phrase am Ende des Tages is learnt as one shape.
sentences.sound: am EN-duh des TAA-gus bin ikh IM-er MUE-duh.

variations.display: Am Ende der Woche bin ich immer müde
variations.cue: At the end of the week I am always tired
variations.changed: des Tages becomes der Woche — the same genitive on a feminine noun, which takes der.

mistake.display: Am Ende von dem Tag bin ich immer müde
mistake.why: von dem is not wrong German, but the fixed phrase is genitive: am Ende des Tages. In a set phrase the genitive is what a reader expects.

sentences.mnemonic: am Ende closes the day the way bis closes the wait.
